title: Ramesh Raskar - The Agentic Web and the Bazaar Era of AI

segments.text: RAMESH RASKAR: Fantastic.
So for some time, we have been in the factory era of AI, where
some large companies would produce
these products in large quantities
and we would just consume them.
But very soon, thanks to AGI and small models and things
running on the edge, things running on your machines,
we're shifting to the bazaar era.
So a lot of our work at MIT is about thinking
about when we'll have billions, maybe
trillions of AI agents on the open web, what
would the internet of AI agents would look like?
And to motivate that, imagine a scenario where Sara in Texas,
in rural Texas, has a health condition.
She goes to her doctor, John, and says, hey,
I have chest pain.
I have comorbidity, and she's just not getting a good answer
from her doctors.
And Dr. John can go on the OpenHive on the open web,
and say, hey, listen, for $100, can somebody
solve the problem for Sara?
And when that happens, billions of agents all over the world
wake up and they say, hey, maybe I can take a piece of this $100.
And they can look at their data if it's
related to corresponding health condition,
start training models, also create a coalition,
start collaborating with each other,
and eventually maybe a handful of them
can solve the problem for Dr. John.
And those, let's say about 10 of them solve together,
those 10 get paid out from the $100 and everybody else
disappears.
And then eventually, Dr. John gets an Expedia-like answer
of how he could help Sara, the patient.
And so what's happening here is not like agents for e-commerce.
This is commerce that's possible because of AI agents.
And Dr. John is not accessing some kind of an amazing health
model, AI model out there, but he's tapping
into a network of intelligence.
And that network is available as a marketplace.
This is what we mean by the internet of AI agents
and the commerce for agents.
So again, we in the mainframe era of AI, a factory era of AI.
But very quickly we're shifting to the PC era.
Some companies are already using agents
within trusted boundaries, the intranet of agents.
But very soon, we'll shift to the internet of agents, where
agents are collaborating and negotiating
with other agents that are well outside the trusted boundaries.
But that's still just for geeks, how we can connect.
That's like the internet.
To go from the internet to world wide web,
we needed HTML and browsers and URLs and all the good stuff.
And project NANDA that originally started at MIT
stands for Networked AI Agents in Decentralized Architecture.
A mouthful.
NANDA for short means joy in Sanskrit,
but also the name of my sister.
All right.
So what does it mean to have billions of agents out there?
And if you take this example I showed you
of commerce that agents will conduct,
I think the closest analogy I can imagine
is high-speed trading, high-frequency trading.
And the reason why high-frequency trading works
is we have a bunch of things.
There is a registry.
There is every merchant, every stock is pre-qualified.
There is somewhat price transparency in how that works.
There is a way to deal with fraud detection and so on.
And all these things also had to be built
for the internet of AI agents.
So this is a massive infrastructure
that's going to come get built for the billions of agents
that are out there.
So anybody here like an OpenClaw fan here.
But OpenClaw is great, but it's only inbound.
It only behaves as a tool.
I cannot call your OpenClaw agent.
It's like having a telephone that
can only make calls outside, but can never receive calls.
So it's a one-way agent, not a bidirectional agent.
So the question is who's going to build this infrastructure,
but a more problematic way to think
about this is whoever builds this infrastructure will also
own it.
So the question for us is, will we
end up in a walled gardens of this internet of AI agents,
or will we get an open and vibrant
and neutral and safe and scalable web for AI agents?
So that's the mission for us for NANDA.
And we think that there are four main bottlenecks.
And if you can solve those four bottlenecks,
there's a chance we can keep the generic as open as today's
internet as opposed to how we see
on the mobile phones like iOS and Android
or Facebook and Twitter, all the walled gardens.
So the four bottlenecks are ICANN/DNS-like structure.
Second is passports and certification.
Third is obvious, it is interoperability.
And fourth is attestation.
So I'll go through this very quickly.
And our group at MIT has been working in this space
for the last 11 or 12 years.
So we've been on this journey of thinking
about what happens after AlexNet when
we have billions of individual AI systems
that are interacting with each other.
And now going forward, within our three main research
problems we need to solve, originally starting at MIT,
but now we have many collaborators, the first one,
as I said, is like the DNS for agents.
The second is knowledge pricing.
We think it's very critical that data models, inference, compute,
all needs to be priced.
Just the way when you hire a candidate,
we can figure out their salary.
And the same way we have to do knowledge pricing.
It's a very beautiful mathematical problem.
Come talk to us.
And the other problem is co-learning.
The last 14 years have been a fantastic progress
in machine learning.
But going forward, we think it's all about machine co-learning,
about how two agents learn from each other.
And when you think about co-learning,
it's not just about agents buying services and transacting,
but they're going to form coalitions,
they're going to negotiate, they're
going to compete for resources, and they have achieve decisions.
And there'll be some alliances.
There'll be some betrayal.
It'll be like the Game of Thrones among agents.
So the other thing we need to do is
we need to have a starting point.
For the web, there was something called Yahoo.
Those of us as old as me.
And Yahoo created a safe space to explore what the web is.
And we need something similar to do that.
So we created something called the NandaTown.
So go check out the town off of MIT websites.
It's kind of a sandbox that allows anybody
to bring enterprise agents, payments, memory.
If you're working on any of these spaces,
you can come to NandaTown and explore this extremely
heterogeneous system, and you have some ethical hackers
there and so on as well.
It's moving very, very quickly.
So I encourage you to explore NandaTown.
And then the research, of course,
works in multiple directions.
Agentic devices, this knowledge, pricing,
co-learning, new forms of agent marketplaces, and so on.
And, of course, this is happening
under a very large tent that involves
large companies and startups and governments and so on.
And more recently, we have this series
of hackathons called NandaHack that are sponsored
by different organizations.
So just go to nandahack.media.mit.edu
to explore it.
Now, when we talk about billions of agents,
we should be thinking about at nation scales.
So what's happening now is thanks to a lot of work
at NandaTown, we're able to work with very large ecosystems.
So for example, in India, we launched
something called Doot, which means messenger,
and a 1.5 billion agents that are not
owned by-- there's no corporate capture
and that run on the identity and payment rails they already have.
City of Boston is also launching with us Boston Agent Initiative.
And I invite you to come and talk
to us about how the civic agents are evolving as well.
And what you'll quickly realize is that today we
are thinking about agents for X, agents for coding,
agents for browsing, agents for debugging, agents for shopping,
and so on.
But we need to flip that and start
thinking about services for agents, X for agents,
infrastructure for agents, compute for agents,
insurance for agent, health care for agents,
education for agents.
Everything that we do in the society
needs to be done for agents.
So I think the open agentic commerce
is going to emerge because intelligence will be discovered,
intelligence will be priced, and intelligence
will be coordinated at scale.
So come join us at nanda.mit.edu.
Thank you.
[APPLAUSE]
